title: What Is Jeonse? Korea's Giant-Deposit Rental System, Explained
html:
If you read about Korean housing for more than five minutes, you will meet the word jeonse (전세). It describes a way of renting a home that barely exists anywhere else, and it is slowly disappearing from Korea too.

In one line

Jeonse is a Korean lease where the tenant hands the landlord a very large lump-sum deposit instead of paying monthly rent, and gets the whole deposit back when the lease ends.

How it works

The deposit is big: usually somewhere between 50% and 80% of the home's market value. A typical lease runs for two years. During that time the tenant pays no rent at all, only utilities. The landlord's "rent" is whatever they earn by using or investing the deposit money. When the lease ends, the full deposit goes back to the tenant.

So a family might hand over, say, 300 million won for an apartment worth 450 million won, live there for two years without paying rent, and then walk away with their 300 million won. For the tenant it feels like forced saving. For the landlord it works like an interest-free loan.

Where the word comes from

Jeon (傳) carries the sense of handing something over, and se (貰) means rent or lease, so the word roughly means "a lease paid by handing over money." Accounts of the system date it back to the 19th century. Korea JoongAng Daily links its spread to the 1876 Japan–Korea treaty, which opened the ports of Busan, Incheon and Wonsan and pushed up demand for city housing.

It became common in the 1960s and 1970s. Korea was urbanizing at high speed, mortgages were hard to get, and interest rates were high. A landlord who collected a large deposit could earn good returns on it, or use it as cheap capital to buy another property. Tenants, in turn, could live in the city without a bank loan.

In the news

Jeonse is shrinking. According to The Korea Times (July 3, 2026), government data showed monthly-rent contracts made up 68.6% of all lease deals nationwide in the first five months of 2026, up 7.6 percentage points from a year earlier. Researchers quoted in the article warned jeonse could eventually fall to around 7% of the rental market. The paper also notes that deposit fraud cases in recent years have damaged trust in the system.

Why does this matter? For decades, many Korean families used jeonse as a stepping stone: save, rent on jeonse, then buy. As jeonse fades, that path to owning a home gets narrower.

The risk nobody mentions on day one

Your deposit is only as safe as your landlord's finances. If the landlord cannot pay it back, recovering the money depends on where you stand among the landlord's creditors, and unpaid taxes can rank ahead of tenants. That is why Koreans check a property's registry and debts before signing.

Don't confuse it with

  • Wolse (월세): ordinary monthly rent, usually with a much smaller deposit.
  • Banjeonse (반전세): a hybrid with a medium deposit plus a lower monthly rent.
  • A security deposit in the US or UK: usually one or two months' rent. A jeonse deposit can be more than half the price of the home.

This article is general information, not financial or legal advice.
